{{Short description|Set of linear codes in coding theory}}
{{Refimprove|date=May 2011}}
In [[coding theory]], the  '''Wozencraft ensemble''' is a set of [[linear code]]s in which most of codes satisfy the [[Gilbert-Varshamov bound]]. It is named after [[John Wozencraft]], who proved its existence. The ensemble is described by {{harvtxt|Massey|1963}}, who attributes it to Wozencraft. {{harvtxt|Justesen|1972}} used the Wozencraft ensemble as the inner codes in his construction of strongly explicit asymptotically good code.

==Existence theorem==

:'''Theorem:''' Let <math>\varepsilon > 0.</math> For a large enough <math>k</math>, there exists an ensemble of inner codes <math>C_{in}^1,\cdots,C_{in}^N</math> of [[Code rate|rate]] <math>\tfrac{1}{2}</math>, where <math>N = q^k  - 1</math>, such that for at least <math>(1 - \varepsilon)N</math> values of <math>i, C_{in}^i</math> has relative distance <math>\geqslant H_q^{ - 1} \left(\tfrac{1}{2} - \varepsilon \right )</math>.

Here relative distance is the ratio of minimum distance to block length. And <math>H_q</math> is the q-ary entropy function defined as follows:

:<math>H_q(x) = x\log_q(q-1)-x\log_qx-(1-x)\log_q(1-x).</math>

In fact, to show the existence of this set of linear codes, we will specify this ensemble explicitly as follows: for <math>\alpha  \in \mathbb{F}_{q^k }  - \{ 0\}</math>, define the inner code

:<math>\begin{cases} C_{in}^\alpha  :\mathbb{F}_q^k  \to \mathbb{F}_q^{2k} \\ C_{in}^\alpha  (x) = (x,\alpha x) \end{cases}</math>

Here we can notice that <math>x \in \mathbb{F}_q^k</math> and <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_{q^k}</math>. We can do the multiplication <math>\alpha x</math> since <math>\mathbb{F}_q^k</math> is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{F}_{q^k}</math>.

This ensemble is due to Wozencraft and is called the Wozencraft ensemble.

For all <math>x, y \in \mathbb{F}_q^k</math>, we have the following facts:
# <math>C_{in}^\alpha  (x) + C_{in}^\alpha  (y) = (x,\alpha x)+(y,\alpha y) = (x + y,\alpha (x + y)) = C_{in}^\alpha  (x + y)</math>
# For any <math>a \in \mathbb{F}_q, aC_{in}^\alpha  (x) = a(x,\alpha x) = (ax,\alpha (ax)) = C_{in}^\alpha  (ax)</math>

So <math>C_{in}^\alpha</math> is a linear code for every <math>\alpha  \in \mathbb{F}_{q^k }  - \{ 0\} </math>.

Now we know that Wozencraft ensemble contains linear codes with rate <math>\tfrac{1}{2}</math>. In the following proof, we will show that there are at least <math>(1 - \varepsilon)N</math> those linear codes having the relative distance <math> \geqslant H_q^{ - 1} \left (\tfrac{1}{2} - \varepsilon \right )</math>, i.e. they meet the Gilbert-Varshamov bound.

==Proof==

To prove that there are at least <math>(1-\varepsilon)N</math> number of linear codes in the Wozencraft ensemble having relative distance <math>\geqslant H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right)</math>, we will prove that there are at most <math>\varepsilon N</math> number of linear codes having relative distance <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right)</math> i.e., having distance <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k.</math>

Notice that in a linear code, the distance is equal to the minimum weight of all codewords of that code. This fact is the [[Linear code|property of linear code]]. So if one non-zero codeword has weight <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k</math>, then that code has distance <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k.</math>

Let <math>P</math> be the set of linear codes having distance <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k.</math> Then there are <math>|P|</math> linear codes having some codeword that has weight <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k.</math>

:'''Lemma.''' Two linear codes <math>C_{in}^{\alpha_1}</math> and <math>C_{in}^{\alpha_2}</math> with <math>\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbb{F}_{q^k}</math> distinct and non-zero, do not share any non-zero codeword.

:'''Proof.''' Suppose there exist distinct non-zero elements <math>\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbb{F}_{q^k}</math> such that the linear codes <math>C_{in}^{\alpha_1}</math> and <math>C_{in}^{\alpha_2}</math> contain the same non-zero codeword <math>y.</math> Now since <math>y \in C_{in}^{\alpha_1},  y = (y_1,\alpha_1 y_1)</math> for some <math>y_1 \in \mathbb{F}_q^k</math> and similarly <math> y = (y_2,\alpha_2 y_2)</math> for some <math>y_2 \in \mathbb{F}_q^k.</math> Moreover since <math>y</math> is non-zero we have <math>y_1, y_2 \ne 0.</math> Therefore <math>(y_1,\alpha_1 y_1) = (y_2,\alpha_2 y_2)</math>, then <math>y_1 = y_2 \ne 0</math> and <math>\alpha_1 y_1 = \alpha_2 y_2.</math> This implies <math>\alpha_1 = \alpha_2</math>, which is a contradiction.

Any linear code having distance <math> <H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k</math> has some codeword of weight <math>< H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k.</math> Now the Lemma implies that we have at least <math>|P|</math> different <math>y</math> such that <math>wt(y) < H_q^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right) \cdot 2k</math> (one such codeword <math>y</math> for each linear code). Here <math>wt(y)</math> denotes the weight of codeword <math>y</math>, which is the number of non-zero positions of <math>y</math>.

Denote

:<math>S = \left \{ y  \ : \ wt(y) < H_q^{ - 1} \left (\tfrac{1}{2} - \varepsilon \right ) \cdot 2k \right \}</math>

Then:<ref>For the upper bound of the volume of Hamming ball check [https://www.cse.buffalo.edu/faculty/atri/courses/coding-theory/lectures/lect9.pdf Bounds on the Volume of a Hamming ball]</ref>

:<math> \begin{align}
|P| &\leqslant |S| \\
&\leqslant \text{Vol}_q \left (H_q^{-1} \left (\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right ) \cdot 2k,2k \right ) && \text{Vol}_q(r,n) \text{ is the volume of Hamming ball of radius } r \text{ in } [q]^n \\
&\leqslant q^{H_q \left (H_q^{-1}\left (\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right ) \right ) \cdot 2k} && \text{Vol}_q(pn,n) \leqslant q^{H_q(p )n} \\
&= q^{ \left (\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right ) \cdot 2k} \\
&= q^{k(1-2\varepsilon)} \\
&<  \varepsilon(q^k-1) && \text{ for } k \text{  large enough } \\
&= \varepsilon N
\end{align}</math>

So <math>|P| < \varepsilon N</math>, therefore the set of linear codes having the relative distance <math>\geqslant H_q^{-1} \left (\tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon \right ) \cdot 2k</math> has at least <math>N - \varepsilon N = (1-\varepsilon)N</math> elements.
